articles.title: AI-generated content gets cited more than human content in Google AI Overviews. That should bother you." published: false
articles.description: A peer-reviewed paper published in the Proceedings of Machine Learning Research (volume 318, Canadian...
articles.body_html:
A peer-reviewed paper published in the Proceedings of Machine Learning Research (volume 318, Canadian Conference on Artificial Intelligence 2026) found something that should make anyone producing content for the web uncomfortable:

AI-generated documents are cited more frequently than human-authored documents in Google AI Overviews, even after controlling for retrieval rank.

The study, by Rustem Kakimov, Xing Tan, Jonathan Gillham, and Narcis Bejtic, proposed a framework for auditing citation behavior in AI-generated search summaries. They applied it to Google AI Overviews on "Your Money or Your Life" queries drawn from the MS MARCO Web Search dataset, which covers topics where accuracy matters most: health, finance, and safety.

What they found

The key finding, quoted from the abstract:

"AI-generated documents are cited more frequently than human-authored documents even after controlling for retrieval rank, with the difference driven primarily by non-retrieved citations and most pronounced at highly ranked positions."

Three things to notice in that sentence:

  1. "Even after controlling for retrieval rank" means this is not a side effect of AI content ranking higher. At the same rank position, AI-generated content gets cited more often than human content.
  2. "Driven primarily by non-retrieved citations" means the AI is pulling in AI-generated content through a path that does not go through normal retrieval. It is finding AI content that does not appear in the organic results and citing it anyway.
  3. "Most pronounced at highly ranked positions" means the bias toward AI content is strongest at the top, where citations matter most for visibility.

Why this happens

The paper does not prove a causal mechanism, but the pattern is consistent with what we know about how LLMs process text. Language models generate text by predicting the most likely next token. When they evaluate which source to cite, they are doing something similar: measuring which passage best fits the response being generated. AI-generated text, which is itself the product of likelihood maximization, tends to match the model's own output patterns more closely than human text does.

A commenter on Hacker News put it plainly: "I can consistently reproduce this by asking Claude which code snippet it prefers: the one it generated in a different chat, or one that I refactored for my own needs and find more useful. It always picks its own."

This is not a bug. It is a structural property of how generative retrieval works. The system that generates the answer also selects the sources, and it has a preference for text that looks like what it would produce.

The Google angle

Google's official AI optimization guide says: "If an AI can write your article on its own, it will never cite you." The guide frames this as advice: produce content that AI cannot generate, and you will be cited.

The Kakimov study suggests the inverse is also true: content that AI can generate is more likely to be cited, because the retrieval system prefers text that matches its own output distribution. The two statements are not contradictory. They describe the same phenomenon from two sides: non-commodity human content gets cited because it is unique, and AI-generated content gets cited because it matches the model's preferences.

The uncomfortable middle is where most content lives: human-written but indistinguishable from what AI would produce. That content gets cited less than both extremes.

What this means for content strategy

The implication is not "use AI to write your content so it gets cited more." That would accelerate a feedback loop where AI generates content, AI retrieves it, and AI cites it, with human voices pushed to the margins.

The implication is that the content most likely to be cited by AI search engines falls into two categories:

Content that AI cannot produce. Original research, first-hand experience, proprietary data, expert analysis with a specific point of view. Google's guide calls this "non-commodity content." The Kakimov study confirms it gets cited because it adds something the model does not already have.

Content that AI produces. AI-generated summaries, listicles, and generic informational content. These get cited because they match the model's output patterns, but they are also the content most likely to be replaced by the AI generating its own response without citing anyone.

The danger zone is the middle. Well-optimized, well-structured, accurate human content that covers the same ground an AI would cover. It is too generic to be "non-commodity" and too human to match the model's preferences. It gets cited less than both extremes.

The feedback loop problem

If AI-generated content is cited more, and citations drive traffic and authority, then AI-generated content accumulates more authority signals over time. Those authority signals feed back into ranking and retrieval. The system rewards the content it produces.

This is the same pattern that Google's own guide warns against when it says "if AI can write your article, it will not cite you." But the Kakimov data suggests the warning is incomplete. AI can and does cite AI-generated content, at rates higher than human content, in the most sensitive query categories.

The researchers highlight "the importance of transparent, measurement-based auditing for understanding citation behavior in generative search systems." They are right. The only way to know whether this bias is growing, stable, or correcting is to measure it continuously. Right now, almost no one is.

What I am doing about it

The audit tool I maintain, geo-optimizer-skill, does not score content on whether it is AI-generated. Detecting AI content reliably is an arms race, and any heuristic I ship will be outdated within months.

What it does instead is score content on specificity signals: original data, first-hand language, specific examples, and citation-worthy passages. Content that scores high on these signals tends to be non-commodity regardless of who wrote it. Content that scores low tends to be the generic informational text that falls into the danger zone.

That is the practical filter. Not "is this AI-generated" but "does this contain something the retrieval system cannot generate on its own." If the answer is yes, it gets cited. If the answer is no, the data says it gets cited less than both the AI content and the original human content, and the gap may be widening.

articles.title: What Are Your Chances of Surviving Resident Evil Based on Your Tech Job?
articles.description: I recently watched the new Resident Evil movie. 🎬  Watching the main character stumble from one...
articles.body_html:
I recently watched the new Resident Evil movie. 🎬

Watching the main character stumble from one disaster into another was absurdly funny and a little heartbreaking. But what impressed me most was his professional commitment. He is a courier, and no matter what happens around him, he never forgets the job: the package must reach its destination.

I will avoid major spoilers here. You can join this discussion even if you have not seen the movie.

But I have to say this first: the main character deserves real credit for his work ethic. He is not a trained superhero. He is an ordinary courier who takes “deliver at all costs” to its absolute limit. That level of professional commitment is genuinely admirable.

So this thought experiment is not making fun of his decision. It uses his commitment as the starting condition:

You are just as dedicated to your profession as he is to delivering that package.

You cannot resign, call in sick, close the ticket, or simply refuse the mission. You still have to do your job and move forward. Your only advantage is the way your profession has trained you to think.

This is not a serious disaster survival guide. It is just a fun career question inspired by a horror movie. 😄

The city is failing. The ticket is still open.

Then I started wondering: what if I were in his place?

I have worked in QA for 15 years. If I carried all those testing habits into an extreme situation, what would my survival rate be?

My answer is: 50%. 🎲

Not because I can fight monsters. I cannot.

My advantage is that a QA engineer rarely trusts a happy path just because somebody says it should work.

QA Might Try to Stop the Story Before It Starts 🧪

Imagine receiving this task:

Deliver the only copy of a critical item into a city that is clearly falling apart. The environment is unknown. The recipient may be offline. There is no backup route.

My first questions would be:

  • Who created this requirement?
  • Is the recipient still online?
  • Why is there only one copy of the critical item?
  • Where is the backup?
  • What is the rollback plan?
  • Why are we continuing the happy path when production is already throwing alerts everywhere?

Without the “you must be as dedicated as the protagonist” rule, the movie might end in ten minutes. I would return the ticket with this comment:

Preconditions are incomplete. The recipient is unreachable. The production environment is unstable. Release blocked.

Unfortunately, our rules say I still have to continue.

This is where testing experience might help. One strange event can be random. Two might require investigation. But when the roads, people, communications, and infrastructure all fail at the same time, a senior QA should recognize a systemic failure.

The answer is not to keep following the original route. Pause that path. Isolate the risk. Find a safer alternative. Then continue the mission.

Why Testing Skills Might Improve My Odds

I would not casually bring a strangely behaving person into my only vehicle.

That would be the survival equivalent of connecting unvalidated, high-risk input directly to the only production environment that still works.

Before entering an unfamiliar building, I would also check:

  • Where is the exit?
  • Is there a second route?
  • Can the door be opened from the inside?
  • What happens if the power fails?
  • Is this plan dependent on a single point of failure?

I would not assume that something is permanently dead just because it fell over once. I would also avoid putting all hope into one sample, one laboratory, one vehicle, or one person.

Fifteen years in QA has taught me at least one thing:

Every critical process without a backup is just waiting for a sufficiently unlucky day.

That is why I give myself a 50% chance.

Testing experience might help me spot danger earlier, challenge bad assumptions, and stop a broken flow. But it cannot solve fitness, luck, limited resources, or unknown biological monsters.

Fifty-fifty is already my optimistic estimate.

QA Could Also Die From QA Habits 🐛

Of course, being a tester does not automatically make someone good at survival.

Our greatest risk is the need to reproduce a bug.

I might escape safely, then suddenly stop and think:

What exactly triggered that mutation? Distance? Time? Sound? Temperature?

Then I would go back to collect logs, record a better video, and attempt a second reproduction.

Or I might reach the exit, notice one unopened door, and say:

The main flow passed. I will test one last edge case before I leave.

At that moment, my survival probability drops from 50% to 5%. 🚨

The most dangerous sentence in QA: “One last edge case.”

What About Your Tech Job? 🧑‍💻

The same rule applies to you. You bring the same admirable professional commitment that the courier brings to his delivery. You cannot end the story by saying, “Not my ticket.” You must keep doing your job while using your professional skills to stay alive.

Every tech role has a possible survival advantage and a potentially fatal professional habit.

Frontend Engineer

They quickly notice that none of the exits provide useful status feedback and the city map violates every basic UX principle.

Unfortunately, they may spend valuable time complaining that the emergency door has no hover state.

Backend Engineer

They try to identify the source of the infection chain and shut down the upstream service.

They may also believe that restarting the core system will somehow fix everything.

DevOps / SRE

They check monitoring, capacity, failover, and backup regions. They would never trust a cure deployed as a single instance.

However, while every alarm in the city is firing, they might still be deciding whether this is a real incident or a broken alert rule.

Security Engineer

They trust nobody, no attachment, and no unknown device. Their isolation instincts may be the strongest of any profession.

They may also enter the most dangerous area just to prove the full impact of a vulnerability.

Data Engineer

They build a model from infection times, locations, and behavior patterns.

First, they must accept that half the data is missing, every source uses a different format, and there is no schema documentation.

Product Manager

They ask for the goal, target user, priority, and success metric before the outbreak begins.

Then, during the evacuation, they ask whether we can add multiplayer collaboration to the MVP.

AI / Agent Engineer

They send one agent to scout ahead and another agent to review the first agent's conclusion.

The biggest risk is that both agents confidently report “Task completed successfully” while the critical package is still sitting where it started.

Your Turn 🎯

Give yourself a survival probability based on your real profession.

You can use this format in the comments:

Role:
Years of experience:
Survival probability:
My biggest professional advantage:
The professional habit most likely to get me killed:
My first survival rule:

Here is mine:

Role: QA / Test Engineer
Years of experience: 15
Survival probability: 50%
My biggest professional advantage: I do not ignore repeated anomalies or trust a single happy path
The professional habit most likely to get me killed: Going back to reproduce the bug one more time
My first survival rule: When every monitor is alerting, pause the main flow, isolate the risk, and roll back

In the ideal ending, I survive the night, preserve the logs, reproduce every critical issue, and submit this bug report:

Severity: Critical
Reproduction rate: 100%
Impact: Entire city
Recommendation: Block the release immediately

The next morning, Umbrella management replies:

Status: Rejected
Reason: Known issue. No fix planned. Does not affect core business.

Known issue. No fix planned. Apparently production can continue.

Again, this is a silly thought experiment, not an actual survival guide. 😂

And every percentage comes with one final condition: do not run into a Tyrant, Nemesis, or any of the franchise's main characters. If you are a random civilian standing next to the protagonists, your survival rate is basically zero. 😂

Now it is your turn:

If you were dropped into Resident Evil and had to rely on your professional skills, what would your survival probability be—and why?

articles.title: The Bug Lives at the Seam, Not in the Logic
articles.description: The encrypted secret was bytes. It round-tripped perfectly in the in-memory store. The unit tests...
articles.body_html:
The encrypted secret was bytes. It round-tripped perfectly in the in-memory store. The unit tests passed. In Postgres, the column was JSON, and bytes is not JSON-serializable. The secret store blew up at the one boundary the in-memory test never crossed.

That was the pattern of the entire v0.2.0 field test on HivePlane. The hard part wasn't the logic — it was the data model and the boundaries. Every defect was a value that was fine in Python and broke one step later, at a persistence seam.

This is the article about tracing each value across every persistence boundary — because the bug lives one boundary further than your unit test.

One defect per seam-type

Defect The value that crossed the seam Where it broke
D-5 Secret ciphertext as bytes Postgres JSON persistence rejected binary
D-7 A desired_specs row keyed by id Second source hit a PK collision — id vs uniqueness
D-8 The kill-switch record existed GET /tools/disabled listed enabled tools — state vs record
D-9 A workload with runs, deleted Raw FK violation 500 instead of a 409 with a reason
#573 A backup manifest pinning alembic_head=0034 Schema head was 0035 — restore against the wrong schema

Read that table as the taxonomy. The seam, not the logic, is where each one failed.

The bytes that broke JSON

D-5 was the cleanest example. The encrypted secret vault stored ciphertext as bytes. In the in-memory store, it round-tripped perfectly. The unit tests passed. In Postgres, the column was JSON, and bytes is not JSON-serializable. The secret store blew up at the persistence boundary — the one place the in-memory test never exercised.

The fix wasn't in the model; it was at the boundary: base64-encode the ciphertext on the way to Postgres, decode on the way back. The model stays bytes. The seam learns to translate. The unit test that uses the in-memory store still passes — and still proves nothing about the seam.

tip: Your in-memory store and your Postgres store share an interface, not a serialization. A value that round-trips in memory can fail at the JSON column. Trace the value across the boundary the in-memory test never crosses.

The second source that broke the first

D-7 was an id-versus-uniqueness confusion. The reconcile loader keyed desired_specs by id. One source worked. A second source, applying the same desired state, hit a primary-key violation — because the row already existed, and the key assumed one source. The uniqueness constraint and the id were the same field, and they meant different things.

The fix is composite keys and idempotent upserts: (source_id, workload_id). A second source is a second row, not a collision. The bug only appears when you have two sources, which is why the single-source field test never caught it.

The enabled tool that was "disabled"

D-8 was a state-versus-record confusion that I still find funny. GET /tools/disabled returned a list that included enabled tools. The kill-switch record existed in the table; the tool was not actually disabled. The endpoint reported the record, not the state. A "disabled tools" list that includes enabled tools is worse than no list — it trains the operator to ignore it.

The fix: the endpoint reports the state, derived from the record and the current tool status, not the record alone. A record of a disable that was later reversed is history, not a current fact.

The FK that returned 500

D-9 was the database teaching me API design. Deleting a workload that had runs returned a 500 — a raw foreign-key violation surfacing as an internal error. The caller got a server error; the operator got no reason. The fix is a 409 with "workload has N runs; delete the runs first or cascade." A constraint violation is a user-facing condition, not a server fault. The seam between the database and the API is where a 500 becomes a 409.

The schema head the manifest lied about

573 was the one that could have been catastrophic. A backup manifest pinned alembic_head to 0034. The live schema head was 0035. A restore would have succeeded — the manifest said the schemas matched — against a database that was one migration ahead. The restore verified the manifest's claim, not the world's truth.

The fix: the restore verifies the actual schema head against the manifest, and refuses a mismatch. A manifest that lies about its own head is a backup that restores you to the wrong version of your own system.

What I learned

Trace each value across every persistence boundary: binary-vs-JSON, global-key-vs-tenant-scope, id-vs-uniqueness, state-vs-record, FK-vs-409, manifest-head-vs-schema-head. A unit test that stops at the seam passes; the bug lives one boundary further. The Postgres-gated tests — the ones CI runs with a database — are the ones that catch it. And a constraint violation is a user condition, not a server fault: the seam between the database and the API is where 500 becomes 409 with a reason.

The v0.2.0 field test runs zero-skip against the real stack with real PostgreSQL — 36/36 scenarios, 67/67 container tests — and the defect ledger (D-1…D-11) is the evidence that the seams, not the logic, were the work. Full receipts in the field-test report and the Docker test report.

  • Field test report (36/36) · Docker report (67/67)
  • Migration guide (v0.1.0 → v0.2.0)
  • State store design

Pick one value in your system and trace it from the model to the Postgres column to the API response. Where does it change shape? That's where your next bug is — and where your unit test stops.

articles.title: Translation Is Not Agreement: Build a Clarification Handshake for Multilingual Chat
articles.description: Machine translation can make a group message readable without making its intent certain. Build a reproducible TypeScript clarification workflow for Tencent RTC Social Messaging with author-only answers, revision checks, explicit notification failures, and verification tests.
articles.body_html:
A multilingual chat can translate every word correctly and still leave someone wondering: Was that a suggestion, a deadline, or a polite refusal?

That uncertainty is not evidence that you are bad at communication—or that translation has failed. Natural languages encode tone, obligation, and context differently. The engineering mistake is treating translated text as if it removed those trade-offs.

This tutorial builds a clarification handshake for a Tencent RTC Social Messaging group:

  1. A reader requests clarification about a specific message revision.
  2. The request records what is unclear without rewriting the original message.
  3. Only the original author can provide the authoritative answer.
  4. Editing the source message supersedes outstanding requests.
  5. Chat-notification failure remains visible instead of destroying the saved request.

Tencent RTC's Social Messaging scenario covers group discussions, communities, rich media, and other social experiences: https://trtc.io/solutions/social-messaging

TUIChat also provides on-demand text-message translation. Its documentation defines supported content types and languages as well as applicable edition limits: https://trtc.io/document/60772

Translation helps the reader understand the text. The handshake below answers a different question: Who gets to confirm what the message meant?

Start with three different kinds of uncertainty

Before adding a button, classify the user's problem:

User uncertainty Appropriate action
“I cannot read this language” Offer documented on-demand translation when supported
“I can read the words, but the intent is ambiguous” Ask the original author for clarification
“This may violate a community rule” Use the moderation or reporting workflow

Combining these paths creates dangerous shortcuts. A translated sentence should not automatically create a task, settle a dispute, or become a moderator's evidence of intent.

Our example UI will therefore place Translate and Ask what this means beside each other. Neither replaces the original message.

Define the protocol before the interface

A clarification request is attached to an exact source revision:

open
  ├── original author answers ──> resolved
  ├── source message changes ──> superseded
  └── requester cancels ───────> cancelled

Delivery of the chat notification is a separate state:

pending -> sent
pending -> failed       // definitely rejected; safe to retry
pending -> uncertain    // timeout or disconnect; do not retry blindly

That separation matters. If the request is saved but sending its notification times out, deleting the request would lose user work. Blindly retrying could instead produce duplicate messages.

The invariants are:

  • A translation is never stored as the author's statement.
  • Only the source-message author can resolve the request.
  • A request cannot silently move to a newer message revision.
  • Notification failure does not roll back the clarification record.
  • An uncertain send requires reconciliation or a deliberate user retry.

Create the reproducible project

Use Node.js 20 or later:

mkdir multilingual-clarification
cd multilingual-clarification
npm init -y
npm install --save-dev typescript tsx @types/node
mkdir src test

Add this test command to package.json:

{
  "scripts": {
    "test": "tsx --test test/*.test.ts"
  }
}

Implement the state model

Create src/clarifications.ts:

export type ClarificationStatus =
  | "open"
  | "resolved"
  | "superseded"
  | "cancelled";

export type NoticeState =
  | "pending"
  | "sent"
  | "failed"
  | "uncertain";

export type QuestionKind =
  | "literal_meaning"
  | "tone"
  | "required_action"
  | "other";

export interface Clarification {
  id: string;
  threadId: string;
  messageId: string;
  messageRevision: number;
  requesterId: string;
  authorId: string;
  kind: QuestionKind;
  note: string;
  status: ClarificationStatus;
  notice: NoticeState;
  createdAt: number;
  answer?: string;
  resolvedAt?: number;
  closedReason?: string;
}

export interface ChatPort {
  sendText(threadId: string, text: string): Promise<void>;
}

export class ChatSendError extends Error {
  constructor(public readonly certainty: "rejected" | "unknown") {
    super(`Chat send ${certainty}`);
  }
}

export class ClarificationService {
  private readonly rows = new Map<string, Clarification>();
  private sequence = 0;

  constructor(
    private readonly chat: ChatPort,
    private readonly now: () => number = Date.now,
  ) {}

  async create(input: {
    threadId: string;
    messageId: string;
    messageRevision: number;
    requesterId: string;
    authorId: string;
    kind: QuestionKind;
    note: string;
  }): Promise<Clarification> {
    if (input.requesterId === input.authorId) {
      throw new Error("Authors do not need a clarification request to themselves");
    }

    const note = input.note.trim();
    if (note.length > 280) {
      throw new Error("Clarification note is too long");
    }

    const id = `clarification-${++this.sequence}`;
    const row: Clarification = {
      ...input,
      id,
      note,
      status: "open",
      notice: "pending",
      createdAt: this.now(),
    };

    // Persist first. Sending a chat message is an external side effect.
    this.rows.set(id, row);
    await this.deliverNotice(id);

    return this.get(id);
  }

  async deliverNotice(id: string): Promise<void> {
    const row = this.mutable(id);

    if (row.notice === "sent") return;
    if (row.notice === "uncertain") {
      throw new Error("Reconcile an uncertain send before retrying");
    }

    row.notice = "pending";

    try {
      await this.chat.sendText(
        row.threadId,
        `Clarification ${row.id} requested for message ${row.messageId}.`,
      );
      row.notice = "sent";
    } catch (error) {
      row.notice =
        error instanceof ChatSendError && error.certainty === "rejected"
          ? "failed"
          : "uncertain";
    }
  }

  resolve(input: {
    id: string;
    actorId: string;
    currentMessageRevision: number;
    answer: string;
  }): Clarification {
    const row = this.mutable(input.id);

    if (row.status !== "open") {
      throw new Error(`Cannot resolve a ${row.status} request`);
    }

    if (input.actorId !== row.authorId) {
      throw new Error("Only the original author may resolve this request");
    }

    if (input.currentMessageRevision !== row.messageRevision) {
      row.status = "superseded";
      row.closedReason = "source_message_changed";
      throw new Error("The source message changed; create a new request");
    }

    const answer = input.answer.trim();
    if (!answer) throw new Error("An answer is required");

    row.status = "resolved";
    row.answer = answer;
    row.resolvedAt = this.now();
    return this.get(row.id);
  }

  sourceRevised(messageId: string, newRevision: number): void {
    for (const row of this.rows.values()) {
      if (
        row.messageId === messageId &&
        row.status === "open" &&
        row.messageRevision !== newRevision
      ) {
        row.status = "superseded";
        row.closedReason = "source_message_changed";
      }
    }
  }

  cancel(id: string, requesterId: string): Clarification {
    const row = this.mutable(id);

    if (row.requesterId !== requesterId) {
      throw new Error("Only the requester may cancel this request");
    }
    if (row.status !== "open") {
      throw new Error(`Cannot cancel a ${row.status} request`);
    }

    row.status = "cancelled";
    row.closedReason = "requester_cancelled";
    return this.get(id);
  }

  get(id: string): Clarification {
    return { ...this.mutable(id) };
  }

  private mutable(id: string): Clarification {
    const row = this.rows.get(id);
    if (!row) throw new Error(`Unknown clarification: ${id}`);
    return row;
  }
}

The ChatPort is intentionally small. It does not invent a Tencent RTC SDK method name. The application adapter should call the documented text-send operation from the Tencent RTC integration you actually use.

Verify authority, revisions, and delivery uncertainty

Create test/clarifications.test.ts:

import assert from "node:assert/strict";
import test from "node:test";
import {
  ChatPort,
  ChatSendError,
  ClarificationService,
} from "../src/clarifications.js";

const baseRequest = {
  threadId: "group-7",
  messageId: "message-42",
  messageRevision: 1,
  requesterId: "reader",
  authorId: "author",
  kind: "required_action" as const,
  note: "Is this optional, or should it be done today?",
};

test("only the original author can resolve a request", async () => {
  const chat: ChatPort = { sendText: async () => {} };
  const service = new ClarificationService(chat, () => 1000);
  const request = await service.create(baseRequest);

  assert.throws(
    () =>
      service.resolve({
        id: request.id,
        actorId: "another-member",
        currentMessageRevision: 1,
        answer: "It is required",
      }),
    /Only the original author/,
  );

  const resolved = service.resolve({
    id: request.id,
    actorId: "author",
    currentMessageRevision: 1,
    answer: "It is optional; tomorrow is also fine.",
  });

  assert.equal(resolved.status, "resolved");
  assert.equal(resolved.answer, "It is optional; tomorrow is also fine.");
});

test("editing the source supersedes an open request", async () => {
  const chat: ChatPort = { sendText: async () => {} };
  const service = new ClarificationService(chat);
  const request = await service.create(baseRequest);

  service.sourceRevised("message-42", 2);

  const current = service.get(request.id);
  assert.equal(current.status, "superseded");
  assert.equal(current.closedReason, "source_message_changed");
});

test("an ambiguous send failure is not retried automatically", async () => {
  let attempts = 0;
  const chat: ChatPort = {
    sendText: async () => {
      attempts += 1;
      throw new ChatSendError("unknown");
    },
  };

  const service = new ClarificationService(chat);
  const request = await service.create(baseRequest);

  assert.equal(request.status, "open");
  assert.equal(request.notice, "uncertain");
  assert.equal(attempts, 1);

  await assert.rejects(
    service.deliverNotice(request.id),
    /Reconcile an uncertain send/,
  );
  assert.equal(attempts, 1);
});

test("a definitely rejected notification can be retried", async () => {
  let attempts = 0;
  const chat: ChatPort = {
    sendText: async () => {
      attempts += 1;
      if (attempts === 1) throw new ChatSendError("rejected");
    },
  };

  const service = new ClarificationService(chat);
  const request = await service.create(baseRequest);

  assert.equal(request.notice, "failed");
  await service.deliverNotice(request.id);
  assert.equal(service.get(request.id).notice, "sent");
  assert.equal(attempts, 2);
});

Run the suite:

npm test

These tests verify the decisions that matter more than the button styling:

  • A fluent bystander cannot speak for the author.
  • An old clarification cannot be applied to edited text.
  • A timeout does not trigger an uncontrolled duplicate send.
  • A definite rejection remains recoverable.

Connect the workflow to TUIChat

Keep translation and clarification as neighboring capabilities rather than one pipeline.

Translation path

For a supported text message, let the user explicitly invoke TUIChat's documented on-demand translation experience. Before enabling it in a deployment, check the official documentation for:

  • supported message content types;
  • supported source and target languages;
  • applicable edition requirements;
  • the platform-specific integration instructions.

Do not copy a language list into application code and assume it will remain accurate. Treat the documentation and your verified deployment configuration as the capability source.

If translation is unavailable, preserve the original message and show an honest state such as:

Translation is not available for this message.
You can still ask the author for clarification.

Clarification path

The Ask what this means action should receive source data from the rendered message:

await clarifications.create({
  threadId: currentThread.id,
  messageId: selectedMessage.id,
  messageRevision: selectedMessage.revision,
  requesterId: currentUser.id,
  authorId: selectedMessage.authorId,
  kind: "tone",
  note: "Does this mean you agree, or that you want more discussion?",
});

The field names above belong to this tutorial's application model. Map them to identifiers and revision tracking that your own backend controls; they are not presented as Tencent RTC API names.

Render the resulting record as a card associated with the source message:

Clarification requested · Tone
“Does this mean you agree, or that you want more discussion?”
Waiting for the original author

When resolved:

Answered by the original author
“I agree with the direction, but not the proposed deadline.”

Do not parse the translated notification text to reconstruct state. The clarification record is the state; the chat message is only a user-visible notification.

Production persistence needs conditional writes

The in-memory map makes the state machine easy to reproduce, but a production backend should perform conditional database updates.

For example, resolving a request should be equivalent to:

UPDATE clarifications
SET status = 'resolved', answer = ?, resolved_at = ?
WHERE id = ?
  AND status = 'open'
  AND author_id = ?
  AND message_revision = ?;

Treat an affected-row count of zero as a conflict, not as success. Another process may have superseded, cancelled, or resolved the request first.

For chat notices, use an outbox worker if requests must survive a server restart. Still retain an uncertain state: a process can lose its connection after the messaging service accepts a send but before the worker records success. Unless your documented integration provides an appropriate deduplication mechanism, do not promise exactly-once notification delivery.

A duplicate notice with the same clarification ID is preferable to two independent clarification records. Clients can collapse notices that point to an already-rendered card.

Failure behavior users can act on

Failure Internal state User-visible response
Translation unsupported Clarification unaffected Keep original visible; offer clarification
Notification definitely rejected notice: failed Show “Request saved; notification not sent” and a retry action
Notification outcome unknown notice: uncertain Show “Request saved; delivery unconfirmed” rather than retrying silently
Source message edited superseded Link to the new revision and offer a new request
Non-author attempts to answer No state change Explain that only the original author can confirm intent
Author deletes the source Close or supersede according to policy Remove quoted content and explain that the source is unavailable
Request contains harassment Moderation path Preserve access controls and allow reporting; translation is not moderation

Two privacy rules deserve particular attention:

  1. Do not copy private message bodies into notifications that have broader visibility.
  2. Recheck thread membership when reading or answering a clarification. Possessing a clarification ID must not grant access to its source conversation.

The engineering judgment that remains valuable

It is easy to frame multilingual tooling as a test of whether a developer knows enough languages. That is not the most useful question.

The durable skill is deciding where certainty comes from:

  • The translation feature can provide a readable rendering.
  • The application can preserve identity, revision, and delivery state.
  • The original author can confirm intent.
  • A moderator can decide whether behavior violates community rules.

Those responsibilities should not collapse into one “smart” message box. Making them visible helps users name uncertainty without feeling that they have failed a language test.

Release verification checklist

Before shipping, verify the complete social-messaging flow:

  • [ ] The original message remains accessible beside any translation.
  • [ ] Translation is user-invoked and enabled only for a verified deployment configuration.
  • [ ] Unsupported content or language combinations have a visible fallback.
  • [ ] Clarification requests store the source message ID and revision.
  • [ ] Only the original author can resolve a request.
  • [ ] Editing or deleting the source invalidates open requests according to policy.
  • [ ] A failed notification does not delete the saved request.
  • [ ] An uncertain notification is not retried automatically.
  • [ ] Database writes use conditional updates to prevent double resolution.
  • [ ] Thread authorization is checked when creating, reading, and answering requests.
  • [ ] Abuse reports remain separate from translation and clarification.
  • [ ] Clients do not treat translated notification text as protocol data.

A multilingual community does not need to pretend every sentence has one mechanically recoverable meaning. It needs a reliable way to move from readable to confirmed when the distinction matters.

Disclosure: I have a content relationship with Tencent RTC. Official Tencent RTC documentation was used as the implementation reference for the product-specific portions of this tutorial.

articles.body_html:
My smart light bulb tried to mine crypto last Tuesday.

Not a joke. Not a metaphor.

I have a cheap Tuya bulb I bought from for $12.99 in 2023. "Smart Life" app, WiFi enabled, 16 million colors, works with Alexa. I put it in my closet so I could say "closet on" and feel like I'm in .

At 3:17 AM, my network monitor woke me up. Not an alarm — just a little red dot on my Grafana dashboard. My closet bulb had uploaded 400MB of data to an IP address in Shenzhen and was now holding a persistent outbound connection on port 3333. Port 3333 is not for turning on lights. Port 3333 is for Monero mining pools.

I unplugged it. I took it apart. Inside was an ESP8266 clone, 2MB of flash, firmware from 2019 with a hardcoded Telnet password: admin:admin. And a little bonus binary called xmr_mini hidden in a partition that shouldn't exist.

That bulb was $13. It had no business having enough brains to betray me, but it did. And it's not alone. Your house is full of them.

Welcome to the Internet of Shit.

The Lie We All Bought

The IoT pitch was beautiful: everything connected, everything smart, everything effortless.

The reality is this: a $400 billion industry built on the cheapest possible chips, running the oldest possible Linux kernels, written by the lowest bidder, shipped with default credentials that haven't changed since 2008.

Here's the math that kills you:

A company wants to sell a smart plug for $9.99.

  • The ESP8266 chip costs $0.89
  • The relay costs $0.40
  • The plastic costs $0.30
  • The profit margin needs to be $4

Where do you think they cut costs? Security audits? Code review? A firmware update server?

No. They cut everything.

They take the SDK example code from Espressif that says // TODO: CHANGE DEFAULT PASSWORD, they don't change the default password, they compile it, and they ship 500,000 units.

I've dumped firmware from 23 different IoT devices in the last year. Light bulbs, cameras, doorbells, pet feeders, a smart toaster — yes, a toaster that can run Doom and also get botnetted.

Here is what I find, every single time:

1. Telnet or SSH open with root:root or admin:admin
In 2026. After Mirai. After 8 years of us screaming about Mirai.

2. A web server running as root from 2016
With a CVE list longer than my grocery list. No update mechanism. Ever.

3. Hardcoded MQTT credentials
One username and password for every device they ever sold. mqtt_user: TuyaSmart123! — I found that in 4 different brands.

4. Cloud buckets with no auth
Your camera footage, your voice clips, your WiFi password — sitting in an open S3 bucket because the intern left public: true in the config.

This isn't a bug. This is the business model.

My Living Room Botnet Census

I got angry after the light bulb thing, so I did what any normal person does: I turned my apartment into a surveillance state for my own devices.

I took that $26 GL.iNet Mango router — the little yellow travel router everyone buys for hotel WiFi — and I made it my border guard.

I flashed it with OpenWrt. Put it between my modem and my real router. Installed:

  • Pi-hole to DNS-blackhole every ad, tracker, and telemetry domain
  • AdGuard Home as backup
  • Suricata in IDS mode to watch what my devices actually say

Then I let it run for 7 days. I didn't block anything. I just watched.

Here is what my "smart" home does when I'm not looking:

My $35 Wyze camera: Pings wyze-log.s3.amazonaws.com every 30 seconds, even when I have "record only on motion" turned off. Uploaded 2.1GB in a week. Of what? I'm not recording 2.1GB of my living room wall.

My smart TV (TCL ): At 2am every night, it resolves 47 different ad domains. It tried to reach doubleclick.net 14,000 times in 7 days. Fourteen thousand. It also sends my WiFi SSID and a list of nearby SSIDs to Roku every 6 hours. Why does Roku need to know my neighbor's WiFi name?

My robot vacuum: Sent a compressed map of my apartment — literally a floorplan of where my bed is — to a server in Singapore. The privacy policy says "to improve cleaning." My bed doesn't need to be in Singapore.

My wife's smart toothbrush: Yes, this exists. It sends brush time, pressure, and location to . 19 times a day.

The worst offender? A $19 smart plug from a brand that doesn't exist anymore. It tried to SSH into my NAS. My own plug tried to brute force my own NAS on my local network. Because its firmware had Mirai's old dictionary baked in and it scans /24s automatically.

We put computers that actively attack other computers inside our houses and then act surprised when they do.

Why Your Router is Lying to You

Your ISP router is not a router. It's a plastic box designed to blink green so you stop calling tech support.

It does NAT. It does WiFi badly. It does not inspect traffic. It does not tell you that your light bulb is mining Monero. It will never tell you.

You need a watchtower.

This is why I tell everyone to build a $20 SOC — Security Operations Center. It sounds insane. SOCs are for enterprises with 6 monitors and cold brew on tap. But a $20 SOC is just a tiny Linux box that sits and judges all your other boxes.

The Mango costs $20-26 on Amazon. Total build with a USB stick for logs is under $30. It draws 2 watts. It has no subscription. It will outlive your smart fridge.

What it gives you:

  • Visibility. For the first time, you see that your bulb is talking to 45.76.123.89 at 3am. That alone is worth it.
  • Blocking at the root. Pi-hole kills ads, trackers, and 80% of malware C2 domains before they even leave your house. Your TV gets dumber — which is good. Dumb TVs can't snitch.
  • Receipts. When that bulb gets popped, you have logs. When you call the manufacturer and they say "impossible," you send them a pcap. They shut up very fast.

The second part of my setup is even more paranoid: an offline box.

I have a Raspberry Pi Zero 2 W — $35 if you're lucky — running a local LLM completely offline. No WiFi, no cloud. I call it the Blackbox. I feed it suspicious firmware dumps, weird log lines, long ToS documents I don't want to upload to ChatGPT. It summarizes, it finds hardcoded creds, it writes abuse emails. Nothing ever leaves my apartment.

When you're dissecting a light bulb that tried to rob you, you don't want to paste its private key into someone else's cloud.

The Fix Isn't What You Think

People want me to say "don't buy smart devices." That's not realistic. I'm not going to hand-wash dishes because my dishwasher has WiFi.

The fix is hostile architecture. Treat every IoT device like it's already compromised, because statistically, it is.

My rules now:

1. VLAN or it didn't happen. All IoT shit goes on its own WiFi network that can't talk to my laptops, NAS, or phones. The Mango makes this 3 clicks. Your main router probably doesn't. That's why you need the Mango.

2. No internet unless it proves it needs it. My light bulbs don't need internet to turn on. I block their internet at DNS level. If they stop working, good — I return them and buy ones that work locally with Home Assistant or ESPHome. If a light bulb requires the cloud to turn on, it's not a light bulb, it's a subscription to light.

3. Flash or trash. If a device runs ESP8266/ESP32, I flash it with Tasmota or ESPHome immediately. Open firmware, local control, no cloud, no mystery binaries. It takes 10 minutes and it turns a spy into a tool. If I can't flash it, I don't buy it.

4. Assume default passwords. First thing I do with any new device: nmap it. nmap -p 23,22,80,8080 <its IP>. If Telnet is open, I try admin/admin, root/root, admin/password. It works 60% of the time. I then change it or brick it.

5. Log everything for 7 days. When you get a new device, put it in the watchtower and just watch. If it phones home 14,000 times, you know.

The IoT industry will not fix itself. There is no incentive. A $13 bulb that is secure costs $15. And $15 loses to $13 on Amazon every time. Security is invisible until it fails, and failure is externalized onto you.

The only person who can secure your house is you. And it doesn't take a $10,000 rack. It takes $26, a USB stick, and the willingness to accept that your smart home is actually a very dumb botnet that you happen to live in.

My closet light is now running ESPHome. It turns on. It turns off. It doesn't mine crypto. It doesn't talk to Shenzhen. It took me 20 minutes to flash.

It is the only smart device in my house I trust.

The rest are in jail.

Want to build the same jail I use?

This is the exact defensive stack from this story — the parts lists, flash commands, Pi-hole blocklists, and Suricata rules I use so my own light bulbs can't betray me:

The $20 SOC: Build a Tiny Defensive Network Monitor — The Mango build, step-by-step. How to put a Pi-hole + IDS between your modem and your whole house, VLAN your IoT, and finally see what your TV does at 2am. My live configs and power measurements inside: numbpilled.gumroad.com/l/20dollarsoxc

BUILD THE BLACKBOX: An Offline AI Field Terminal That Works When Nothing Else Does — The Pi Zero that runs Phi-3/Gemma locally with no cloud. I use it to dissect firmware, parse logs, and draft abuse reports without ever sending your home data to OpenAI: numbpilled.gumroad.com/l/blackbox-offline-ai

articles.body_html:
It started with a text message at 11:47 PM.

Your USPS package could not be delivered. Please confirm address within 12 hours: usps-resolve-helpdesk[.]com/track

I don't have a USPS package coming. I know it's a scam. You know it's a scam. My mom would click it.

I usually delete these. This time I didn't. I was bored, I was wired on bad coffee, and I had a fresh Kali VM open.

I decided to click back.

Hour 0: Building The Cage

Rule #1 if you're going to poke scammers: never do it from your real life.

I spun up what I call my cage. It's not fancy:

  • A Mullvad VPN exit in another state
  • A Firefox profile that has never logged into anything real, running in a VM with no access to my files
  • A burner email from SimpleLogin, a Google Voice number that forwards to nowhere
  • Burp Suite open, recording everything

I clicked.

The site was a perfect clone of USPS. Good CSS, good logo, even the tracking animation. It asked for my address and a $1.45 redelivery fee. Classic.

I put in fake data. 123 Fuckyou Lane, Charlotte NC. The burner email. And a fake card number from Stripe's test card list: 4242 4242 4242 4242. Any payment form that accepts that without a Stripe test mode is not talking to Stripe. It's talking directly to a Telegram bot or a panel.

It accepted it. Of course it did.

Then it said "Payment Failed - Try Another Card." And it asked again.

That's the tell. They don't want $1.45. They want you to burn through 2-3 real cards trying. Each attempt is logged.

I checked the page source. The form action was posting to https:// usps-resolve-helpdesk[.]com/api/verify.php. Not USPS. Obvious. But inside that JS file was something less obvious:
A hardcoded Telegram bot token. In client-side JavaScript.

Amateur hour. Or they just don't care because they burn domains every 48 hours anyway.

I saved the token. I didn't touch the Telegram API yet — that's crossing a line from OSINT into unauthorized access. But I now had a thread to pull.

Hour 8: Day 1 - Who Are You?

I ran the domain.

Registered 2 days ago on Namecheap with privacy guard. Hosted on a cheap VPS in Moscow, ASN 203...something. Cloudflare in front of it.

But the phishing kit itself had left metadata. The favicon was /favicon.ico?v=usps2024 — same string I found in 11 other domains on URLScan.io. Same kit author.

I pivoted on URLScan. Found 3 other live clones:

  • dhl-express-fix[.]com
  • tolls-ezpass-pay[.]com
  • chase-secure-alert[.]com

Same kit, same Telegram exfil structure, same bad opsec.

The scammer was running multiple campaigns off the same infrastructure. This wasn't a lone kid. This was a small operation.

I fed the burner email I used into HaveIBeenPwned, Dehashed, IntelX. Nothing. But the phone number I gave them? Within 4 hours I got a call.

Indian accent, call center noise in background. "Hello, this is USPS, we are calling about your package, your card did not work..."

I answered with a voice changer. "Oh thank god, yeah my card..."

He wanted me to read the card number over the phone. I gave him another fake one, slowly. He typed it. I heard him swear in Hindi when his own checker said invalid.

Then he got angry. "Madam, why you are wasting my time?"

That was the first time it got personal. He knew. He'd flagged me as a time-waster. Most people hang up here.

I apologized and said I was confused. He softened, went back to script. He asked for my real name to "verify the address."

I said "Lusynth." He paused. "What kind of name is that?"

Now it was really personal.

Hour 24: Day 2 - The Flip

I stopped playing victim and started playing bigger fish.

I sent a message to the burner number from another burner: "Hey bro, your USPS panel is showing token in source. You should fix. Also your Cloudflare is leaking origin IP via email headers when you send the smishing."

I was bluffing on the second part. But it's true 70% of the time.

He replied in 11 minutes: "who is this"

I said: "I buy logs. You have US logs? I saw your domain on Telegram. I want to buy."

This is how the ecosystem works. The kid who smishes is often not the guy who cashes out. He sells the "logs" — fullz — to someone else for $5-$15 each.

He sent me a Telegram handle. Not his personal — a business account with 2,300 subscribers. @usps_logs_live. Bio: "Fresh USPS/DHL/Chase - $8 per log - bulk - escrow"

Bingo. This was his storefront.

I joined with a sock puppet Telegram account. His channel had screenshots of "successful logs" — credit cards with last 4, bank names, victims' zips. One was from Charlotte. 28262. My zip code.

That one hit weird. Someone 10 minutes from me got hit by this exact guy and now their card is in his inventory.

I scraped the channel history with a Telegram export. 4 months of posts. I found patterns:

  • He posted mostly 9am - 6pm IST. So India timezone.
  • He always used the same Bitcoin address for escrow.
  • He reused the same username on a blackhat forum from 2023: desi_hustler_99.

I took that username and ran it through Sherlock, WhatsMyName. Found a GitHub. Found a now-deleted YouTube channel that taught "ethical hacking" with the same voice from the phone call.

He was 19. From his GitHub commits, learning Python from a course. His real name was in a commit email.

I'm not going to share it. That's doxxing and it's not the point. The point is, for 5 hours I had turned a random smishing text into a whole person.

And I felt sick.

Not because he was a mastermind. Because he wasn't. He was a kid who learned requests library 6 months ago and realized he could make more in a day scamming than his dad makes in a month. And he was good at it enough to hurt real people near me.

Hour 52: Day 3 - Shutting It Down Without Becoming Him

This is where most "I hacked the scammer" stories turn into revenge porn. They delete his files, they swat him, they leak his data. That's not justice, that's just becoming a different kind of criminal and getting your Medium account banned.

What actually hurts these operations is boring, unsexy, defensive work.

Here's what I did:

1. Killed the infrastructure. I reported the origin IP and domains to Cloudflare Abuse, Namecheap, and the host's abuse@ with full logs, headers, and the Telegram bot token. I also reported the Telegram bot to @botfather and the channel to Telegram abuse. Cloudflare dropped him in 6 hours. Namecheap suspended the domain in 12. His Telegram bot stopped responding by hour 60. His business is gone for that week.

2. Poisoned his logs. All those fake cards I fed him? I kept feeding them. 40 fake submissions over 72 hours from different fake personas via a simple Python script + Selenium. Every fake log he tries to sell now makes him look like a scammer to other scammers. His reputation on his own channel tanked. People started calling him rippper in comments.

3. Protected my own perimeter. I took that Charlotte victim zip as a warning. I rebuilt my home network trap. This is where my real work lives.

I don't use a normal router anymore. I use a little $26 travel router that runs OpenWrt — the GL Mango. I flashed it and put it between my modem and everything else. It runs Pi-hole to kill tracking and ad domains, and a tiny IDS that logs whenever an IoT device talks to a weird IP at 3am. It has saved me twice.

And I have a second box — a Pi Zero that runs a fully offline LLM. No cloud, no API keys. I use it to parse logs, summarize abuse reports, and draft the emails to hosting providers without ever sending victim data to OpenAI. When you do this kind of work, the last thing you want is to leak a victim's PII into someone else's training set.

What 72 Hours Actually Taught Me

Scammers aren't hackers. They're businessmen with bad code. Their opsec is terrible. They reuse passwords, they leave tokens in JS, they use the same BTC address. You don't need to be a 0-day god to beat them. You need to be patient and systematic.

The infrastructure is the product. Taking down one domain does nothing. Taking down his Telegram bot, his Cloudflare front, and poisoning his reputation does. Attack the business model, not the kid.

It will feel personal, and that's the trap. When you hear someone from your own city got hit, when the guy mocks your name, you want revenge. Revenge makes you sloppy and makes you cross lines that will get you in trouble. Document, report, sinkhole. Don't hack back.

Your family is the real attack surface. That USPS text wasn't aimed at me. It was aimed at my mom, your mom, anyone who is tired and expects a package. The best defense isn't your fancy EDR. It's a 10-minute conversation with your family: "The USPS will never text you for $1.45. If you're unsure, forward it to me."

I didn't save the world in 72 hours. I probably cost one 19-year-old about $400 in lost sales and a weekend of rebuilding his kit. He'll be back next week with a new domain.

But one domain gone means maybe 30 fewer people in 28262 get that text tonight. That's enough for me.

Don't try to be a hero. Be a speed bump.

Want the build notes for the defensive setup I used in this story?

I keep all the actual how-to stuff — the firmware, wiring, flash commands, blocklists, and offline AI setup — off Medium and in two guides I update constantly:

The $20 SOC: Build a Tiny Defensive Network Monitor — How I turned that GL.iNet Mango into a full Pi-hole + IDS + logging box that catches exactly this kind of IoT exfil and smishing infra. Parts list, flash steps, my configs: numbpilled.gumroad.com/l/20dollarsoxc

BUILD THE BLACKBOX: An Offline AI Field Terminal That Works When Nothing Else Does — The Pi Zero box that runs a local LLM with no internet, so you can analyze sketchy logs and write abuse reports without leaking anything to the cloud: numbpilled.gumroad.com/l/blackbox-offline-ai
