articles.description: One thing I think frontend engineers need to be more deliberate about is how we apply software design...
articles.body_html:
One thing I think frontend engineers need to be more deliberate about is how we apply software design principles when building component-based applications.

There is a tendency to treat co-location, separation of concerns, reusability, and Atomic Design as though they all mean the same thing: breaking code into smaller pieces and organizing those pieces into folders. They do not. Each principle addresses a different problem, and misunderstanding the distinction can lead to abstractions that look reusable on the surface but become increasingly difficult to maintain.

1. Co-location is about proximity, not combining everything into one component

Co-location means keeping code close to the part of the application it relates to. The underlying idea is that code that changes together should generally be located together.

For example, suppose a feature has a component, its validation schema, feature-specific hooks, helper functions, and tests. Keeping those things within the feature's module makes it easier to understand, modify, and maintain that feature without navigating an unrelated collection of global folders.

But co-location does not mean combining all those responsibilities into one component or file.

Consider a password input that is used only by an authentication feature. It makes sense to keep its implementation close to the authentication feature while it remains specific to that context. If it eventually becomes useful across multiple features, we can extract it into a shared UI module.

The important distinction is that co-location determines where code belongs; separation of concerns determines what responsibilities that code should have.

These principles complement each other. They do not compete.

2. Separation of concerns is about responsibility

Separation of concerns means dividing a system into units with clearly defined responsibilities. A component should have a coherent purpose and a contract that makes its behavior understandable.

Consider a generic input component. Its responsibility might include rendering a native input, forwarding standard input attributes, supporting accessibility, and applying the design system's styling.

Now imagine extending that same component to handle all of the following:

  • Standard text inputs.
  • Password inputs with visibility toggles.
  • OTP inputs with multiple digit slots.
  • Grouped inputs with prefixes, suffixes, or multiple fields.
  • Input-specific validation, formatting, keyboard navigation, and specialized error handling.

We could expose a type prop and several additional flags, then use conditional statements to decide which implementation to render.

That might appear efficient because everything is available through one component. However, the component is gradually taking responsibility for several different interaction patterns, each with its own state, behavior, accessibility requirements, and testing needs.

The problem is not simply that the file has become large. The deeper problem is that its interface and implementation are now responsible for too many distinct concerns.

A change to OTP navigation should not require us to reason about password visibility. A change to password visibility should not risk breaking the behavior of an ordinary text field.

A shared component should provide a stable foundation, not become a container for every component that happens to involve an input.

3. Atomic Design helps us reason about the level of abstraction

Atomic Design provides a useful vocabulary for organizing interfaces into atoms, molecules, organisms, templates, and pages.

A basic input can be treated as an atom: a foundational UI primitive. A form field combining a label, input, and error message can be treated as a molecule. A larger form section combining several fields, validation feedback, and submission controls might be an organism, depending on its scope and complexity.

However, Atomic Design is a mental model, not a rigid classification system. The correct level of abstraction depends on what a component does, what it depends on, and how it is used.

For example:

  • Input: A generic, reusable primitive with a clearly defined contract.
  • PasswordInput: A specialized component that composes the generic input with password-specific behavior, such as a visibility toggle.
  • OTPInput: A specialized component that manages multiple digit positions, focus movement, and keyboard interactions.
  • InputGroup: A composition that combines an input with adjacent elements, such as a prefix, suffix, or action.
  • FormField: A higher-level composition that associates a control with its label, description, and validation feedback.

These are not necessarily five atoms. They operate at different levels of abstraction.

The goal is not to create a separate component for every possible variation. The goal is to ensure that each abstraction represents a coherent responsibility and that higher-level components build on lower-level primitives rather than forcing every behavior into one primitive.

4. Composition is how we build specialized behavior without bloating foundational components

Composition allows us to build complex interfaces by combining smaller components with well-defined responsibilities.

Instead of making the generic Input component understand every possible input pattern, we can build specialized components around it.

For example:

function PasswordInput(props: InputProps) {
  const [visible, setVisible] = useState(false);

  return (
    <div className="password-input">
      <Input
        {...props}
        type={visible ? "text" : "password"}
      />

      <button
        type="button"
        onClick={() => setVisible((value) => !value)}
        aria-label={visible ? "Hide password" : "Show password"}
      >
        {visible ? <EyeOff /> : <Eye />}
      </button>
    </div>
  );
}

This is a simplified illustration, but it demonstrates the architectural distinction: the generic input remains responsible for rendering an input, while the password component owns the additional password-specific interaction.

The OTP input can have its own implementation for digit management, focus movement, and keyboard behavior. It may reuse the same design tokens, styling conventions, and lower-level primitives without forcing the generic input to implement OTP-specific logic.

Likewise, an input group can compose a generic input with prefixes, suffixes, or action buttons.

The objective is not to eliminate conditional rendering. Conditional rendering is perfectly reasonable when it expresses a genuine variation within a component's responsibility. The problem arises when a component becomes a large conditional dispatcher for unrelated behaviors.

Composition gives us a way to reuse implementation without coupling every consumer to every other use case.

React supports this through component nesting, children, and explicit props. A component can provide a structural foundation while allowing its consumer to determine what content or specialized component belongs inside it.

5. Reusability does not mean putting every use case behind one API

A common architectural mistake is assuming that if two components share a visual element, they should necessarily be represented by one highly configurable component.

But visual similarity does not always imply behavioral similarity.

A password input, an OTP input, and a grouped input all involve inputs, but their interaction models differ substantially. Their shared foundation does not justify merging their responsibilities.

A better approach is to reuse at the appropriate level:

  • Reuse design tokens for consistent spacing, typography, colors, and sizing.
  • Reuse generic primitives for common rendering and styling.
  • Compose specialized components from those primitives where it makes sense.
  • Keep feature-specific behavior within the feature that owns it.
  • Promote a feature-specific abstraction into a shared module when there is a genuine need for broader reuse.

This also avoids premature abstraction. A component does not need to become globally available simply because it has been written once. Reuse should emerge from a clear contract and a real need, rather than from the desire to eliminate every instance of duplication.

6. Component boundaries and code splitting are related, but they are not the same thing

There is another important distinction here.

Keeping unrelated implementations together can make architectural boundaries harder to understand and maintain. It can also contribute to unnecessarily large bundles when the module dependency graph causes code to be included together.

However, putting components in separate files does not automatically guarantee code splitting. Modern bundlers determine chunks from the import graph, build configuration, and dynamic import boundaries.

If an OTP implementation is only needed on a particular route, a deliberate dynamic import or lazy-loaded feature boundary may allow that code to be loaded separately. Merely extracting OTPInput into its own file does not guarantee this result.

The architectural benefit of separation is that it gives us clearer units of responsibility and makes independent loading, testing, and evolution easier to reason about. The bundler still needs the appropriate module boundaries to produce the desired output.

We should avoid confusing a good component architecture with an automatic performance optimization.

7. Why this matters even more in the AI era

AI can generate components, refactor files, create abstractions, and reproduce patterns very quickly. But generating code that works is not the same as designing a system that remains maintainable as it grows.

If we ask an AI tool to build a reusable input component without defining the intended boundaries, it may produce a single component with a long list of props, conditional branches, and flags to accommodate every foreseeable use case.

That implementation may work. It may even look elegant in a small example. But it can introduce hidden coupling, unclear contracts, and unnecessary complexity as more requirements are added.

The problem is not that AI inherently produces poor architecture. It is that AI needs architectural constraints and evaluation criteria, just as a human engineer does. Without them, local convenience can take precedence over the long-term structure of the application.

This is where engineering principles become more valuable, not less.

A design system should do more than standardize colors, spacing, typography, and component appearance. It should also establish rules for component responsibility, composition, dependency direction, state ownership, and reuse.

For example, a design system should make the following expectations explicit:

  • Foundational UI primitives should remain focused on their core responsibilities.
  • Specialized interactions should be composed from existing primitives where appropriate.
  • Feature-specific logic should remain close to the feature that owns it.
  • Shared components should expose clear, strongly typed contracts.
  • New abstractions should be introduced when they address a real need, not merely to make code appear more reusable.
  • Generated code should be reviewed for architectural fit, not only whether it renders correctly.

These rules give an AI coding tool a set of constraints against which to evaluate its own implementation. They also make code review more objective because the team can assess whether the implementation follows an agreed architectural model rather than relying solely on individual preferences.

Conclusion

Good component architecture shouldn't be about creating the smallest possible components or the fewest possible files. It should be about finding the right boundaries between responsibilities.

Co-location tells us where related code should live. Separation of concerns tells us which responsibilities should remain distinct. Atomic Design gives us a vocabulary for understanding levels of UI abstraction. Composition gives us a mechanism for building richer interfaces from focused components.

When these principles are applied together, a design system becomes more than a collection of reusable UI elements. It becomes an architectural contract that helps developers and AI tools build software that can evolve without accumulating unnecessary complexity.

articles.title: The Inbox Autopilot: What 60 Days of Letting an n8n Workflow Triage My Email Taught Me
articles.description: The Inbox Autopilot: What 60 Days of Letting an n8n Workflow Triage My Email Taught...
articles.body_html:
The Inbox Autopilot: What 60 Days of Letting an n8n Workflow Triage My Email Taught Me

This is part of my build-in-public series on running LLM workflows in n8n in production. Everything here is from a real template I sell and support â the mistakes are mine, the fixes are tested.

The 45 minutes nobody budgets for

Every morning I did the same thing: open Gmail, scan 60â80 new emails, decide what needed a reply, what could wait, and what was noise. It took 45 minutes on a good day. Not writing replies â just deciding. The triage, not the work.

So I built a workflow to do the deciding. A Gmail trigger, a classifier, a draft-reply generator, and a morning review. It's been running for 60 days. It now saves me about 35 minutes every morning. But the interesting part isn't the time saved â it's the three ways it failed, each of which taught me a rule I now apply to every classifier I build.

The architecture (one paragraph)

Gmail Trigger on new mail â a Code node that strips signatures, disclaimers, and quoted history â a classifier LLM call that assigns one of five buckets: urgent, needs-reply, waiting-on-me, newsletter, noise â a confidence gate â for needs-reply, a second LLM call drafts a reply in my voice â drafts land in Gmail as drafts, never sent. Urgent gets a Slack/Telegram ping. Newsletters get auto-archived. The morning review is a Gmail search: in:draft newer_than:1d, five minutes, approve or edit.

The one hard rule: the workflow never sends email. Draft-only. That single constraint makes every other failure recoverable.

Failure #1: the confident misclassification

Week two, a customer wrote in with a refund request. Long email, polite tone, order number buried in paragraph three. The classifier filed it as newsletter with 0.91 confidence.

Why? My few-shot examples were synthetic â tidy little emails I wrote myself, each fitting its bucket perfectly. Real email is not tidy. The model learned "polite + long = newsletter" from my examples and confidently applied it.

The fix was to throw away the synthetic examples and few-shot with my real email â 40 actual messages, warts and all, including the ones where a refund request reads like a thank-you note. Accuracy on the tricky cases went from "scary" to "boring." Synthetic examples teach the model a clean world that doesn't exist.

Failure #2: the tone-deaf draft

Classification fixed, drafting began. The first week of drafts were grammatically fine and emotionally wrong. An annoyed customer got a cheerful "Happy to help! ð" reply. A formal partner email got slang.

The problem: one system prompt for all drafts. The fix: per-bucket tone templates. The drafting prompt receives the bucket and a one-line voice card: needs-reply-angry â "acknowledge the frustration first, no exclamation marks, no emojis, state what happens next"; needs-reply-formal â "use their name, sign with full signature." It's not fancy, but misfire rate on tone dropped to near zero. Voice is a parameter, not a personality.

Failure #3: thread blindness

This one cost me a customer interaction. Someone replied to an existing thread; the workflow classified the single message â "Sounds good, let's do it" â as noise. It was a purchase confirmation for a $79 custom service request. The purchase-confirmation context lived three messages up, which I'd stripped as "quoted history" to save tokens.

Lesson: strip quoted history for classification, but fetch the thread for context when it matters. Now the classifier gets the current message plus the last two messages of the thread (compressed), which costs ~300 extra tokens and catches every "sounds good" that actually means something. Token savings that break decisions aren't savings.

The confidence gate (the part I'd copy anywhere)

Every classification returns a confidence score. Below 0.75, the email goes into a sixth bucket: unsure â always shown to the human, never auto-filed. The unsure bucket gets 10â15% of mail, and that's by design: it's where the classifier admits ignorance instead of being confidently wrong. I'd rather review 12 emails than un-archive one misfiled refund.

This is the same pattern as the review-queue and retry-budget posts in this series: the system's honesty about its own limits is the feature. A classifier without an unsure bucket is a liar with good PR.

The cost math

~70 emails/day, classification at ~600 tokens each plus drafts for ~10 of them: about $0.40/day on GPT-4o-mini. The 35 minutes it saves me every morning would need to be worth $0.40. It is. The Gmail API is free, n8n is self-hosted, and the only real cost was the week I spent fixing the three failures above.

What I kept manual

Two things deliberately stay human: the final send (I read every draft before it goes â the 5-minute morning review is the whole quality system), and the unsure bucket (which is a human inbox by another name). Everything else â reading, sorting, drafting, archiving â is the workflow's. That split has held for 60 days without an incident worth mentioning, which for an email automation is the highest praise I have.

I'm building AI Automation Lab â production-ready n8n workflow templates. The AI Inbox Triage & Reply Drafter is the full workflow from this article: the Gmail trigger, the classifier with real-email few-shots, the confidence gate, the per-bucket draft templates, and the morning-review setup. My open-source patterns live at github.com/zhp910318/n8n-ai-automation-lab.

articles.title: Build an invoice reminder workflow in n8n with Google Sheets (idempotent, AU GST wording)
articles.description: Build an invoice reminder workflow in n8n with Google Sheets (idempotent, AU GST wording)
articles.body_html:
Flow: Schedule Trigger (daily 9am, workflow timezone set) → Google Sheets "Get rows" → Code node (decide) → Send Email (SMTP) → Google Sheets "Update row" (match on row_number).

The decision logic

  1. Skip rows where status is paid, cancelled or on hold.
  2. daysFromDue = today − due_date, where today is the date in the workflow timezone: $today.toFormat('yyyy-MM-dd'), not new Date().toISOString(), which gives the UTC date (at 9am in Sydney that's still yesterday, so every count comes out a day short). Accept YYYY-MM-DD and DD/MM/YYYY text plus Google Sheets serial numbers, and reject impossible dates instead of letting Date.UTC roll them over.
  3. Stages = [−3, 0, 7, 14, 30]. Pick the highest stage whose offset ≤ daysFromDue, so downtime doesn't cause a burst of emails.
  4. Send only if that stage's index is greater than the stored last_stage_sent index (idempotent).
  5. Write back last_stage_sent and last_sent_date.

Gotchas we hit

  • Send Email v2.1 appends an n8n attribution footer by default. Turn it off under Options.
  • Importing with n8n import:workflow fails if the JSON has no id.
  • Test against a local SMTP catcher (e.g. Python aiosmtpd) before touching a real inbox.
  • Google Sheets can hand you a date cell as a serial number (46312 is 17 Oct 2026), depending on the Get rows node's Options → Output Formatting → Date Formatting. A five-digit number matches neither text pattern, so a reformatted column quietly drops out of the reminders. We set that option to Serial Number explicitly and convert it (snippet below).
  • The email goes out before last_stage_sent is written, so if Update row fails, the next run sends the same stage again. Turn on Retry On Fail for the Update row node and set an Error Workflow so you hear about it. 
const todayStr = $today.toFormat('yyyy-MM-dd'); // workflow timezone, not UTC
const today = new Date(todayStr + 'T00:00:00Z');
const EPOCH = Date.UTC(1899, 11, 30); // Google Sheets / Excel day zero
const ymd = (y, m, d) => { const t = new Date(Date.UTC(y, m - 1, d));
  return t.getUTCMonth() === m - 1 && t.getUTCDate() === d ? t : null; };
function parseDate(v) {
  const s = String(v ?? '').trim(); let m;
  if (typeof v === 'number' || /^\d{5}(\.\d+)?$/.test(s)) { const n = Number(s); // Sheets serial
    return n > 20000 && n < 80000 ? new Date(EPOCH + Math.floor(n) * 86400000) : null; }
  if ((m = s.match(/^(\d{4})-(\d{1,2})-(\d{1,2})/))) return ymd(+m[1], +m[2], +m[3]);
  if ((m = s.match(/^(\d{1,2})\/(\d{1,2})\/(\d{4})$/))) return ymd(+m[3], +m[2], +m[1]); // DD/MM/YYYY
  return null;
}
const daysFromDue = due => Math.round((today - due) / 86400000);

AU GST wording

If the business is GST-registered: "Tax invoice … Total includes GST of $X", where X = total ÷ 11 rounded to the cent. Otherwise: "Invoice … No GST has been charged".

Updated 17 Oct 2026: added the timezone, serial-date and write-back notes after a reader's comment. Thank you.

Packaged version with guide, sample sheet and 5 templates: https://ledgerlinetools.gumroad.com/l/au-invoice-chaser

Published by Ledgerline Tools, a small Australian automation studio. Questions: ledgerlinetools@proton.me

articles.title: An incident report nobody could open, an extension that wanted my token, and 80 lines instead
articles.description: The report nobody could open   We write incident reports as single HTML files: inline CSS,...
articles.body_html:
The report nobody could open

We write incident reports as single HTML files: inline CSS, an inline SVG timeline, no build step, one file you can read in ten years. They live in a private GitHub repository next to the code they are about.

Nobody could open them. GitHub shows an .html file as source, and the "download it, then double-click it" workflow is where reading stops for most people. GitHub Pages would render them, but Pages on a private repository is an Enterprise feature. GitHub's PDF viewer exists, but these are not PDFs.

The extension that wanted my token

There is a Chrome extension for exactly this problem. I read its code before installing it. It asks for a GitHub token (a personal access token, or an OAuth grant with full repo scope), sends that token to the author's server, and the server fetches your file and renders it on the author's domain.

That is a lot of trust for a preview button. An incident report is the most sensitive document a team writes, and the fix was to hand the key to the whole repository to a stranger's Lambda.

The other option, a userscript, keeps the token in the browser but resolves the short-lived tokenised link GitHub issues for a private file and passes it, as a URL parameter, to the author's website, which loads the file from there. The link to your private file lands in that site's address bar, history and hosting logs.

Both are honest projects, and the idea of a button beside Raw is theirs. I just did not want the file to leave the browser.

The Raw button already does the hard part

Click Raw on a private file and watch the network tab. GitHub answers github.com/<owner>/<repo>/raw/<ref>/<path> with your own session, then redirects to raw.githubusercontent.com with a token that expires in minutes. That host serves the file as text/plain, which is why it is never rendered, and sends Access-Control-Allow-Origin: *. And github.com's Content Security Policy allows connections to it.

So a script running on the file page can do what Raw does, and then fix the only thing that was wrong, the content type:

const tab = window.open('', '_blank');                    // open inside the click, so popup blockers allow it
const response = await fetch(location.pathname.replace('/blob/', '/raw/'), { credentials: 'same-origin' });
const html = await response.text();
tab.location.href = URL.createObjectURL(new Blob([html], { type: 'text/html' }));

That is the whole mechanism. The only network request is the one GitHub itself makes for Raw. No server, no token, no account, no site other than github.com in the path. The rendered page lives at a blob: URL in your browser, with no cookies and no access to GitHub.

80 lines instead

The result is unraw: a userscript that adds an unraw button next to Raw on every .html file page, and a bookmarklet for people who do not want to install anything. The button copies Raw's classes and data-* attributes so it matches GitHub's current styling, and a MutationObserver puts it back after GitHub's client-side navigation. The rest is the snippet above with error handling. Your userscript manager shows you all of it before installing; it is about 80 lines.

Two limits, both inherent to the approach. Pages that reference relative files (./style.css, img/x.png) render without them, because those paths do not exist at a blob: URL; self-contained pages render completely, and inlining is the right habit for documents you want to read from GitHub anyway. Inline scripts run inside the blob: page, isolated from GitHub, so treat a preview the way you would treat opening a downloaded copy.

The rule that produced the tool is the rule that keeps it small: the file may not leave your browser. Anything that would need a server or a token will not be added.

  • Install page, with the bookmarklet: https://thangaram611.github.io/unraw/
  • Userscript on Greasy Fork: https://greasyfork.org/scripts/600316-unraw
  • Source, MIT, with a comparison table drawn from each tool's code: https://github.com/thangaram611/unraw

articles.title: Copy a remote video into R2 from a Cloudflare Worker without buffering it
articles.description: If your Worker copies files it didn't create (AI generation results, imports from a URL, exports from...
articles.body_html:
If your Worker copies files it didn't create (AI generation results, imports from a URL, exports from another service), the obvious line, await res.arrayBuffer(), loads the whole file into an isolate whose 128 MB is shared by every request it is serving. For video that's the wrong default. You can stream the file straight from the source into R2 instead, and it takes three pieces: FixedLengthStream, pipeTo, and an S3 PUT signed as UNSIGNED-PAYLOAD.

The code below is trimmed from the copy step at Movoa, which moves each finished video from a provider's temporary URL into our own bucket.

TL;DR

  • Workers memory is 128 MB per isolate, not per request, so buffered copies add up across concurrent requests.
  • Stream when the source sends Content-Length: response.body.pipeTo(new FixedLengthStream(length).writable) and PUT the readable side.
  • Sign the stream with aws4fetch; it uses UNSIGNED-PAYLOAD, which R2's S3 API accepts over HTTPS.
  • Reject tiny bodies before writing, and fall back to buffering only when there's no length (or you're in Node).

Why buffering is the trap

The tempting version is three lines:

const res = await fetch(resultUrl);
const body = new Uint8Array(await res.arrayBuffer());
await bucket.put(key, body);

Cloudflare's limits page (read 2026-10-16) is specific about why this bites: each isolate "can consume up to 128 MB of memory", and "this limit is per-isolate, not per-invocation. A single isolate can handle many concurrent requests." When an isolate goes over, in-flight requests are allowed to finish and new requests go to a fresh isolate; under heavy load some incoming requests can be cancelled.

So the risk isn't one big file. It's two or three ordinary video files being copied by the same isolate at the same moment, each fully materialised in memory.

The PUT needs a length, so stream only when you have one

A single S3 PUT to R2 wants a Content-Length. A raw ReadableStream doesn't carry one, which is where FixedLengthStream comes in. It's a Workers runtime TransformStream that you construct with the expected byte count: it tells the runtime the body's length up front, and it errors if the bytes that flow through don't match. That second property is a truncation check: if the source sends fewer than length bytes, the stream errors and the upload fails instead of leaving half a file in your bucket.

Here is the streaming branch, lightly trimmed from our code:

const response = await fetch(url, {
  headers,                 // forward auth if the result URL needs it
  redirect: 'follow',
  signal: AbortSignal.timeout(timeoutMs),
});
if (!response.ok || !response.body) return fail(`HTTP ${response.status}`);

const contentType = response.headers.get('content-type') || 'application/octet-stream';
const length = Number(response.headers.get('content-length') || NaN);

const FixedLength = (globalThis as any).FixedLengthStream; // only exists on workerd
if (FixedLength && Number.isFinite(length) && length > 0) {
  if (length < minBytes) {
    void response.body.cancel().catch(() => {});
    return fail(`too small (${length} bytes)`);
  }
  const { readable, writable } = new FixedLength(length);
  const piping = response.body.pipeTo(writable);   // source → FixedLengthStream
  const result = await putStream(env, { body: readable, length, key, contentType });
  await piping.catch(() => {});                    // surface nothing twice
  return result;
}

Two details matter. The pipeTo promise is started but not awaited before the PUT, because the PUT is what drains the readable side; awaiting the pipe first would deadlock. And the feature check on globalThis.FixedLengthStream keeps the same module working under Node in local dev, where that class doesn't exist (more on that below).

Signing a body you haven't read

R2 speaks the S3 API, so the PUT is a signed request. SigV4 normally includes a hash of the payload, which is impossible for bytes you haven't received yet. aws4fetch handles this by signing a stream body as UNSIGNED-PAYLOAD, and R2 accepts that over HTTPS:

import { AwsClient } from 'aws4fetch';

// env: R2_ACCESS_KEY_ID, R2_SECRET_ACCESS_KEY (an R2 API token),
// R2_ENDPOINT = https://<account-id>.r2.cloudflarestorage.com, R2_BUCKET
async function putStream(env, { body, length, key, contentType }) {
  const client = new AwsClient({
    accessKeyId: env.R2_ACCESS_KEY_ID,
    secretAccessKey: env.R2_SECRET_ACCESS_KEY,
    region: 'auto',
    service: 's3',
  });
  const res = await client.fetch(`${env.R2_ENDPOINT}/${env.R2_BUCKET}/${key}`, {
    method: 'PUT',
    headers: {
      'Content-Type': contentType,
      'Content-Length': String(length),
    },
    body,                              // the FixedLengthStream readable
  });
  if (!res.ok) {
    const detail = (await res.text().catch(() => '')).slice(0, 200);
    return fail(`Upload failed: ${res.status} ${detail}`);
  }
  return { success: true, key, url: publicUrlFor(key) };
}

Checks before you write anything

  • A 200 that is really an error. Some providers answer the result URL with a short JSON error and a 200 status when a file isn't ready or has expired. A minBytes threshold checked against Content-Length catches that before anything is written; cancel the body so the connection is released.
  • Redirects and auth. Signed result URLs often redirect to object storage. Set redirect: 'follow' and pass through whatever headers the provider requires.
  • Timeouts. AbortSignal.timeout(ms) on the fetch keeps a stalled source from holding the request open indefinitely. We give the whole download-and-upload 100 seconds.

What about the R2 binding?

If your Worker has the bucket bound (env.BUCKET), put() accepts a ReadableStream too. The catch is the same: the stream needs a known length, which a fetch() response body with a Content-Length has, and the readable side of a FixedLengthStream has. So await env.BUCKET.put(key, response.body) streams when the source sends a length; for anything else, wrap it in FixedLengthStream first.

We use the S3 API instead because the same storage module also runs under Node (local dev and scripts), where there is no binding, and one signed-request path serves both.

When you can't stream

Two cases still take the buffered path:

  1. The source sends no Content-Length (chunked transfer). Without a length there's nothing to give FixedLengthStream, and a single PUT can't be sent. Buffering is the simple answer; for large files, a multipart upload with fixed-size parts is the scalable one.
  2. Local development under Node (next dev, next start), where FixedLengthStream isn't defined. The feature check routes these to arrayBuffer(), which is fine on a laptop. 
// No length, or not on workerd: buffer, and know this is the memory path.
const body = new Uint8Array(await response.arrayBuffer());
if (body.length < minBytes) return fail(`too small (${body.length} bytes)`);
return uploadFile({ body, key, contentType });

Checklist

  • Check response.ok and Content-Length before touching storage.
  • On workerd with a known length: pipeTo into new FixedLengthStream(length), PUT the readable side, then settle the pipe promise.
  • Sign with aws4fetch (UNSIGNED-PAYLOAD); send Content-Length explicitly.
  • Reject bodies under a sane minimum; follow redirects; set a timeout.
  • Buffer only as the fallback, and treat it as the path that costs memory.

On the streaming branch the file never sits in your isolate's memory, and a short read fails loudly instead of saving half a video. The buffered branch is the exception you keep for chunked sources and local dev.

The videos this copies come from the Movoa video generator, which turns one sentence or a photo into a clip with sound; the first one is free and needs no account.

articles.title: Add a Link Preview Smoke Test to Your Deploy Pipeline (Node Script + GitHub Actions)
articles.description: We test our APIs, our components, and sometimes our CSS. Then a release goes out, marketing drops the...
articles.body_html:
We test our APIs, our components, and sometimes our CSS. Then a release goes out, marketing drops the new page into a Slack channel and a LinkedIn post, and the card shows last month's image with a title that ends in "| Home".

Link previews break silently. No error page, no failed request in your logs, nothing in Sentry. The first signal is usually a screenshot from someone outside the team. So I started treating the share card like any other contract and testing it after deploy.

This post walks through a small, dependency-free Node script that checks the Open Graph and Twitter Card tags on a list of production URLs, plus a GitHub Actions job that runs it after each deploy.

What's worth asserting

You don't need to test everything in the <head>. The failures I see most often are:

  1. og:title, og:description, or og:image missing from the first HTML response (often because they're set client-side).
  2. og:image is relative, points at localhost or a staging host, or doesn't return an image.
  3. Duplicate og:title / og:image tags from two plugins or two layout levels.
  4. og:url pointing at the wrong environment.
  5. twitter:card missing when you actually want the large image layout on X.

All of those are visible in raw HTML, which is exactly what crawlers read. Most social crawlers don't execute JavaScript, so the test shouldn't either. A plain fetch is closer to reality than a headless browser.

The script

Save this as scripts/check-previews.mjs. It uses Node 18+'s built-in fetch, so there's nothing to install.

// scripts/check-previews.mjs
const BASE = process.env.SITE_URL ?? "https://example.com";
const PATHS = ["/", "/pricing", "/blog/latest-post"];
const UA = "Mozilla/5.0 (compatible; PreviewSmokeTest/1.0)";

function metaAll(html, key) {
  // Matches property="og:x" or name="twitter:x", either attribute order
  const re = new RegExp(
    `<meta[^>]+(?:property|name)=["']${key}["'][^>]*>`, "gi");
  return [...html.matchAll(re)].map((m) => {
    const c = m[0].match(/content=["']([^"']*)["']/i);
    return c ? c[1] : "";
  });
}

async function checkImage(url) {
  const res = await fetch(url, { headers: { "User-Agent": UA }, redirect: "follow" });
  const type = res.headers.get("content-type") ?? "";
  const size = Number(res.headers.get("content-length") ?? 0);
  return { ok: res.ok && type.startsWith("image/"), status: res.status, type, size };
}

async function checkPage(path) {
  const url = new URL(path, BASE).toString();
  const res = await fetch(url, { headers: { "User-Agent": UA } });
  const html = await res.text();
  const errors = [];

  for (const key of ["og:title", "og:description", "og:image", "og:url"]) {
    const values = metaAll(html, key);
    if (values.length === 0) errors.push(`${key} missing`);
    if (values.length > 1) errors.push(`${key} appears ${values.length} times`);
  }

  const [image] = metaAll(html, "og:image");
  if (image) {
    if (!image.startsWith("https://")) errors.push(`og:image not absolute https: ${image}`);
    if (/localhost|staging|vercel\.app/.test(image)) errors.push(`og:image points at non-prod host: ${image}`);
    else {
      const img = await checkImage(new URL(image, url).toString());
      if (!img.ok) errors.push(`og:image fetch failed (${img.status}, ${img.type})`);
      if (img.size > 1_000_000) errors.push(`og:image is ${Math.round(img.size / 1024)} KB`);
    }
  }

  const [ogUrl] = metaAll(html, "og:url");
  if (ogUrl && !ogUrl.startsWith(BASE)) errors.push(`og:url is ${ogUrl}`);

  if (metaAll(html, "twitter:card").length === 0) errors.push("twitter:card missing");

  return { url, status: res.status, errors };
}

const results = await Promise.all(PATHS.map(checkPage));
let failed = 0;
for (const r of results) {
  if (r.status !== 200 || r.errors.length) {
    failed++;
    console.error(`âœ— ${r.url} (HTTP ${r.status})`);
    r.errors.forEach((e) => console.error(`   - ${e}`));
  } else {
    console.log(`âœ“ ${r.url}`);
  }
}
process.exit(failed ? 1 : 0);

Run it locally against production:

SITE_URL=https://yoursite.com node scripts/check-previews.mjs

A few design choices worth calling out:

  • Regex instead of a DOM parser. For <meta> tags in a server-rendered head this is good enough and keeps the script dependency-free. If your HTML is unusual (unquoted attributes, tags split across lines with odd spacing), swap in node-html-parser or cheerio.
  • Duplicate detection. Two og:image tags is one of the most common real-world bugs, especially with CMS plugins or nested layouts. Crawlers pick one, and it's often not the one you want.
  • The size check uses content-length. Some servers don't send it for images; that's fine, the check just passes. Tighten it if you care.
  • twitter:card is enforced. X can fall back to Open Graph for title, description and image, but the card layout itself comes from twitter:card. If you want summary_large_image, say so. Delete that line if you don't post to X.

Running it after every deploy

The test has to hit the deployed site, so it belongs after your deploy step, not in the unit test job. Here's a minimal GitHub Actions workflow triggered after a successful deployment:

# .github/workflows/preview-smoke.yml
name: Link preview smoke test
on:
  deployment_status:
  workflow_dispatch:

jobs:
  previews:
    if: github.event_name == 'workflow_dispatch' || github.event.deployment_status.state == 'success'
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v4
      - uses: actions/setup-node@v4
        with:
          node-version: 20
      - run: node scripts/check-previews.mjs
        env:
          SITE_URL: ${{ github.event.deployment_status.environment_url || 'https://yoursite.com' }}

Hosts like Vercel and Netlify emit deployment_status events, so this runs automatically for previews and production. For preview deployments, you may want to relax the "non-prod host" rule, since the image URL will legitimately point at the preview domain.

What the script won't tell you

An automated check proves the tags exist and the image loads. It doesn't tell you whether the card looks right: whether the headline gets cut off mid-word, whether the important part of the image survives a wide crop, whether the description reads like a sentence or a keyword list.

For that, I still eyeball the card before any launch that matters. I use OG Scope, a free checker I built for this. Paste the public URL and it fetches the HTML server-side (no JavaScript, same as the crawlers), then shows estimated cards for LinkedIn, WhatsApp, Facebook, X, Slack, Discord and Telegram, a metadata table, an image check, and a short checklist. No account needed. The cards are estimates, not the platforms' own renders, so for a stale cache you still go to Facebook's Sharing Debugger or LinkedIn's Post Inspector.

The split works well in practice: the script guards against regressions on every deploy, and a human looks at the card when the stakes are high.

Extending it

Ideas once the basic version is running:

  • Read PATHS from your sitemap so new pages get covered automatically.
  • Assert og:title length (around 60 characters is a reasonable ceiling before truncation).
  • Check that og:image changed when your hero image changed, to catch stale cached URLs.
  • Post failures to a Slack channel instead of only failing the job.

It's a tiny amount of code for a bug class that otherwise only gets reported by your users. Worth an afternoon.

Abid Ali is a web developer in Pakistan who builds small developer tools. He made OG Scope to check link previews before they go out.

articles.title: The Search Engine With Zero Server Calls
articles.description: A prebuilt JSON index, weighted AND matching, ARIA combobox - site search with no server, no dependencies, no round-trips. ~1,000 pages.
articles.body_html:
Every search box you've ever shipped came with the same tax: a search endpoint, a spinner, a payload, and - if you took the SaaS route - a service that bills monthly to index what is usually a few hundred names the page could have shipped with in the first place.

I run The DJ Calendar, a site of roughly 1,000 pages covering DJs, venues and shows. Its site search has never had a server. No endpoint, no spinner waiting on a round-trip, no monthly bill. It's a JSON index rendered into the page at deploy time and a small scoring function that runs in the browser on every keystroke.

I've now extracted that whole pattern into a standalone, MIT-licensed repo: instant-search-index. Zero dependencies. One JS file. This post is how it works and, because that's where the real lessons live, what broke along the way.

The opinion underneath it

Most search boxes are infrastructure cosplay. A request to a search endpoint, a spinner, a payload - for a catalog of a few hundred records.

My stance: if the catalog fits in the page, the search belongs in the page. Ship the index as JSON, score it in the browser on every keystroke, and the search feels instant because it is instant. There is no network left to wait on.

There's a second property I care about even more than speed: the index is generated, not queried. It's built at deploy time by the same PHP that renders the artist pages, so the search index and the page content come from the same data. A search index that drifts from the pages it links to is worse than no search at all - this one can't drift, because it's rendered from the source, not synced to it.

The index contract

One JSON array per page. Three searchable fields, two display-only ones:

{
  "title": "Carl Cox",
  "subtitle": "Techno / House",
  "keywords": "techno house icon ibiza space",
  "badge": "Artist",
  "url": "/artists/carl-cox"
}
  • title - the primary match surface, weighted heaviest
  • subtitle - displayed right-aligned, lightly searchable
  • keywords - the synonym field: genre names, city names, whatever users type that isn't literally in the title
  • badge and url - display only; url is where Enter navigates

The keywords field is the quiet hero. Users type "edm", the record says "Tiësto". The keyword field is where you encode everything a human might type that the title will never contain - and it's also where accent folding happens, because folding happens once at index-build time, in PHP, and the client stays ASCII-simple forever. That's why "tiesto" finds Tiësto and "kolsch" finds Kölsch without a single line of Unicode normalization in the browser.

Scoring: AND semantics, weighted by where the match lands

Every keystroke scores every record. A record must match every query token somewhere, or it drops out - AND semantics, not OR. Type "house mafia" and you get Swedish House Mafia and nothing else.

Where a match lands decides the rank:

Signal Weight Example
Title token, exact 60 "cox" hits Carl Cox
Title token, prefix 40 "ame" hits Ame*lie* Lens
Keyword, exact 30 "techno" hits the genre field
Keyword, prefix 18 "tech" hits "techno"
Subtitle, exact / prefix 12 / 8 useful, not the point
Loose substring 4 the safety net
Full-phrase hit +25 "black coffee" beats token soup

The core of the scorer:

var W = { titleExact: 60, titlePrefix: 40, keywordExact: 30,
          keywordPrefix: 18, subtitleExact: 12, subtitlePrefix: 8,
          substring: 4, phraseBonus: 25 };

function scoreEntry(entry, queryTokens, rawQuery) {
  var total = 0;
  for (var i = 0; i < queryTokens.length; i++) {
    var best = bestFieldScore(entry, queryTokens[i]);
    if (!best) { return 0; }        /* one miss kills the record */
    total += best;
  }
  if (entry.haystack.indexOf(rawQuery) !== -1) { total += W.phraseBonus; }
  /* Shorter titles win ties */
  return total * 1000 - entry.record.title.length;
}

That last line is my favorite trick in the file. Two sort priorities - score, then shorter title - get packed into a single integer: multiply the score by 1000, subtract the title length. No comparator object, no tie-break loop, no second pass. It's arithmetic doing the work of a sort policy.

Ties after that fall to index order, which keeps results stable while you type - the list doesn't reshuffle under your fingers mid-word, and mid-word stability matters more than people think. Type "ame" and watch the list: if entries jump around per keystroke, users stop trusting it.

Tokens are precomputed once at load - per-record token arrays for title, subtitle and keywords - so a keystroke scores prepared arrays and never re-splits a string. On the demo's 99 records that's microseconds per keystroke. You'd need six figures of records before this design complains.

The combobox: keyboard is first-class, not an afterthought

The input is a real ARIA combobox, wired properly:

input.setAttribute("role", "combobox");
input.setAttribute("aria-expanded", "false");
input.setAttribute("aria-controls", listId);
input.setAttribute("aria-autocomplete", "list");

Results live in a role="listbox"; arrow keys move an aria-activedescendant pointer; Enter goes to the active option - and here's the detail I'm proudest of: if a query produces exactly one result, Enter goes straight there. No need to arrow down to the only item on screen. The keyboard path is as short as the mouse path.

Two more details that took iteration:

Escape everything before rendering. Matched text gets wrapped in a mark tag, but the title is escaped first - index entries are data, not markup. If an artist were ever named like a script tag, the search box would display it, not run it.

The debounce is 80ms, not the tutorial's 300. Debounce in most search boxes exists to protect a server you're about to annoy. There's no server here. The 80ms is only there to batch keystrokes into one render; the scoring itself is cheap enough to run on every input event.

What broke

The dropdown that vanished. The search widget was perfect in isolation and invisible in production: the results list rendered inside hero containers with overflow: hidden, which quietly amputated everything below the fold of the header. The fix was overflow: visible on every hero and header parent - and a rule I've repeated since: the search box is rarely where the bug is. The page around the search box is the bug farm.

The AND decision I almost reversed. The instinct is to fall back to OR matching when AND finds nothing: "you searched for X, maybe you meant these loosely related things." I left it out. AND plus an honest "No matches." beats OR plus a wall of tangential results, because the top of the list is the product - a confident zero communicates more than a desperate eight.

The payload, stated honestly. The index ships inside the page, which means the page carries it. Hundreds of records is trivially fine - this is a few kilobytes of JSON. But this pattern has a boundary, and the boundary is not where you'd panic: it's when your catalog stops being "names a human can scan" and starts being "a dataset". At tens of thousands of records, close the laptop and use a real engine. Most sites - including most sites that paid for one - are nowhere near that line.

Extracting it

The repo ships the engine, the CSS, and a demo where you can search the real DJ Mag Top 100 the way the production site does - including a "Show how each result scored" toggle that exposes the actual math behind each ranking. No stand-ins; the demo runs the same engine, the same weights, the same defaults as production.

Usage is one line, either declarative (the index travels in the attribute, the widget builds itself):

<input type="text" data-instant-search='[
  {"title": "Carl Cox", "subtitle": "Techno", "keywords": "techno house icon", "url": "/artists/carl-cox"}
]'>

or programmatic, for records that arrive at runtime:

InstantSearch.attach(inputEl, records, { maxResults: 6 });

The numbers

  • 0 dependencies, 0 server round-trips, 1 JS file
  • ~60 lines of scoring core (320 with comments and the combobox)
  • Microsecond scoring on hundreds of records, per keystroke
  • ARIA combobox semantics, full keyboard navigation, escaped output
  • Running in production across ~1,000 pages since 2015

The pattern is instant-search-index on GitHub, with a live demo - type something, then put the mouse away and use the arrow keys.

articles.title: I'm 13 and I built a free calorie tracker. It's live, and here's everything that broke.
articles.description: Every calorie app I tried wanted my email and a card before it showed me anything. So I built one...
articles.body_html:
Every calorie app I tried wanted my email and a card before it showed me anything. So I built one that doesn't.

I don't write code by hand. I describe what I want to Google AI Studio and it writes it. Then I test it on my phone, find what's broken, describe the fix. That's the loop. Two weeks of it.

The app is called ForkCount. forkcount.github.io

What it does

It asks your height, weight, age, gender, and activity level. Then it works out your BMR (Mifflin-St Jeor), your TDEE, and a calorie target that keeps you above your BMR floor. If you try to set a target below that line, it shows you the numbers and explains why.

The rest is a food diary, water tracker, weight log, exercise log, weekly meal plan generator, and a community feed. You type "200g chicken and 150g rice" and it parses the food. No card. No trial. No paywall. No email — just a username and password.

Stack

  • React + Vite + TypeScript
  • Firebase Firestore
  • Firebase Auth
  • GitHub Pages, deployed from the docs/ folder
  • No backend. All logic is client-side.

The bug that cost me the most time

Firestore rejects any document that contains an undefined value anywhere inside it. Not null — undefined. And when it fails, it doesn't tell you which field. It just says:

Function setDoc() called with invalid data. Unsupported field value: undefined

If you're saving a nested object with 40 fields, you're searching for a needle in a haystack. I spent days on this. Fix one field, redeploy, same error for a different one.

The fix was a recursive cleaner, routed through every Firestore write:

function cleanForFirestore(obj) {
  if (Array.isArray(obj)) return obj.map(cleanForFirestore);
  if (obj instanceof Date) return obj;
  if (obj && typeof obj === 'object') {
    const out = {};
    for (const k in obj) {
      if (obj[k] !== undefined) out[k] = cleanForFirestore(obj[k]);
    }
    return out;
  }
  return obj;
}

Then I wrapped setDoc, updateDoc, and addDoc in a helper that cleans every write. One import change, and no write in the app can send undefined to Firestore again.

The second bug: GitHub Pages was serving my source files

The site broke with this:

Failed to load module script: Expected a JavaScript-or-Wasm module script but the server responded with a MIME type of "application/octet-stream"

I stared at the code for two days. The problem was in GitHub Pages settings. It was serving my repo root — which has /src/main.tsx — instead of my built dist/ folder. The fix was to copy dist/ into a docs/ folder, point Pages at /docs, and stop letting it serve source.

The error was the browser refusing to run a TypeScript file as JavaScript. Once I knew that, it made sense.

What I'd like feedback on

  • Does the onboarding flow make sense the first time you see it?
  • Is the calorie calculation right? Mifflin-St Jeor for BMR, activity multiplier for TDEE, 300–500 deficit, floor at BMR.
  • Does it break on your phone?

I'm 13 and I built this by directing AI Studio, not by writing code by hand. If something looks like a beginner mistake, it probably is. Tell me and I'll fix it.

forkcount.github.io

articles.title: I couldn't change the quality of Facebook Reels, so I built a Chrome extension that can
articles.description: Lately I've been hooked on AI-made short films. The Vietnamese channels that translate them keep...
articles.body_html:
Lately I've been hooked on AI-made short films. The Vietnamese channels that translate them keep getting copyright strikes on YouTube, so I started watching them on Facebook instead. Then a new annoyance appeared: halfway through a reel, Facebook would quietly drop the quality to 540p, then 360p. On a fast connection. And Reels has no quality setting at all.

So I built one. Reel Quality is a small Chrome extension that adds a ⚙ button to the reel you're watching, lists the resolutions that reel actually has, and lets you pick one.

  • Chrome Web Store: https://chromewebstore.google.com/detail/nbgnfkagjipmlfhlpilandmenjmilmcc
  • Source (MIT): https://github.com/trieuluan/reel-quality-for-facebook

Transparency note: I built this with a lot of help from an AI coding assistant (Claude Code), and it also helped me edit this post. The debugging on real Facebook pages, the design decisions and the bugs are mine.

Here's how it works under the hood, because it turned out to be more interesting than I expected.

1. Where do the qualities come from?

Facebook plays Reels with DASH over Media Source Extensions. The <video> element only has a blob: URL, so there's nothing to swap. But the page receives a DASH manifest for every reel, embedded in its GraphQL responses as a dash_manifest string (an MPD XML document). Each <Representation> in it is one quality, with a FBQualityLabel like 720p, its own BaseURL, and byte ranges for the init segment and the segment index.

The extension runs a content script in the page's MAIN world at document_start, wraps fetch and XMLHttpRequest, and scans JSON responses for dash_manifest. The first reel's data is server-rendered into <script type="application/json"> tags, so those get scanned too.

One fun surprise: facebook.com enforces Trusted Types, so DOMParser is off the table. The MPD is simple enough that a few regular expressions parse it reliably.

2. Which manifest belongs to which video?

The page holds manifests for several reels at once, so I needed to tie each one to its <video>. The chain I ended up with:

  1. Facebook's player downloads a segment whose URL path matches a BaseURL from some manifest. I remember the response's byte length.
  2. The player appends a buffer of that same length to a SourceBuffer.
  3. That SourceBuffer belongs to a MediaSource, which was turned into the blob: URL that sits in video.src. 
const appendBuffer = SourceBuffer.prototype.appendBuffer;
SourceBuffer.prototype.appendBuffer = function (data) {
  const entry = recentSizes.get(data?.byteLength);
  const ms = entry && sbToMs.get(this);
  if (ms) msToEntry.set(ms, entry);
  return appendBuffer.call(this, data);
};

Hooks on URL.createObjectURL and MediaSource.prototype.addSourceBuffer fill in the other two links. If the chain ever fails, the /reel/<id> in the address bar is a decent fallback.

3. Facebook won't switch quality, so don't ask it to

This was the key decision. Facebook's player reads the manifest once and picks a quality on its own, and there's no public way to tell it otherwise. Rewriting its internals felt fragile.

Instead, the extension lays its own <video> over Facebook's and plays the chosen quality there, video only. Facebook's player keeps running underneath and still owns the sound, the controls, looping and seeking. My layer just follows its clock:

const drift = me.currentTime - fb.currentTime;
if (Math.abs(drift) > MAX_DRIFT) {
  me.currentTime = fb.currentTime;            // big jump: seek
} else {
  const rate = fb.playbackRate * (1 - drift); // small drift: nudge the speed
  me.playbackRate = Math.min(fb.playbackRate * 1.25, Math.max(fb.playbackRate * 0.75, rate));
}
// Only show the HD layer when it is actually in sync; otherwise Facebook's picture shows through.
me.style.opacity = inSync ? '1' : '0';

That last line is what makes it feel seamless: you never get a black frame while the HD layer is buffering, you just see Facebook's own picture for a moment.

4. A tiny DASH player

Each Facebook representation is a single fragmented MP4 with a sidx box (segment index). Read the sidx and you know exactly which byte range holds which seconds of video:

for (let i = 0; i < count; i++, p += 12) {
  const size = v.getUint32(p) & 0x7fffffff; // referenced_size
  const duration = v.getUint32(p + 4);      // subsegment_duration
  segments.push({
    start: time / timescale,
    end: (time + duration) / timescale,
    range: { start: byte, end: byte + size - 1 },
  });
  byte += size;
  time += duration;
}

From there it's a small loop: fetch the init segment, then keep about 20 seconds buffered ahead of Facebook's current time with range requests, and trim what's behind.

5. Bonus: landscape clips stuck in vertical reels

A lot of reels are really a horizontal clip pasted into a 9:16 frame, with black bars and a caption on top. Version 1.1 spots those and can show the clip large in the middle of the screen.

My first version looked at one frame and searched for bright rows. It failed badly on a night-time clip, where most of the "clip" was as black as the bars. The fix was to gather evidence over several frames instead:

  • Bars stay black and never change.
  • Captions in the bars are bright but rarely change.
  • The clip changes almost all the time, even when it's dark.

So each pixel tracks its maximum brightness and how often it changes. Rows that move are clip rows. Then the band snaps to a common aspect ratio (16:9, 1.85, 2.39…); if it's shorter than 16:9, part of a dark clip was probably mistaken for bars, so it falls back to a centered 16:9 window. Finally, everything outside the band has to look like bars, or it's just a normal vertical reel and the option stays hidden.

Honest limitations

  • While a fixed quality is selected, Facebook still streams its own copy underneath, so bandwidth goes up by roughly 25–30%. On Auto, the extension does nothing at all.
  • Facebook changes its internals often. When it does, this will break until I fix it.
  • Desktop Chromium browsers only. Mobile browsers don't run extensions.

Try it

  • Chrome Web Store: https://chromewebstore.google.com/detail/nbgnfkagjipmlfhlpilandmenjmilmcc
  • GitHub: https://github.com/trieuluan/reel-quality-for-facebook

It collects no data and asks for no extra permissions. If you find a reel where it doesn't work, an issue on GitHub would help a lot. And I'd love to hear how you'd have approached the "can't control the player" problem differently.

articles.title: How to check your own IBKR statement for revenge trades
articles.description: Your broker shows a monthly total. It does not show which habit produced it.  I don't have a public...
articles.body_html:
Your broker shows a monthly total. It does not show which habit produced it.

I don't have a public track record to show, so the example below uses a made-up statement: 88 closing trades over four weeks, generated with random P&L and a deliberate penalty for trades right after a loss. Treat the numbers as an illustration of the method, not as real trading results.

On that file, 10 trades closed within 15 minutes of a loss. Together they lost $953, which is -$95 per trade. All 78 other trades averaged +$49 each. The month still ended at +$2,896, so the monthly total hid the pattern.

Here is the method, so you can run it on your own file.

1. Export the right file

In IBKR: Performance & Reports, Statements, Activity, run as CSV. The file has a Trades section. Each row with DataDiscriminator = Order is one fill. Rows with ClosedLot repeat the same fill at lot level, so skip them or you count twice.

2. Keep only closing trades

A closing trade has a non-zero Realized P/L. Opening trades show 0.

3. Flag the ones that follow a loss

Sort closing trades by time. Walk through them and remember the time of the last loss. Any closing trade within 15 minutes of that time goes in the "after a loss" group. Everything else is the baseline group.

let lastLoss = null, after = [], rest = [];
for (const t of closes) {
  if (lastLoss !== null && t.time - lastLoss <= 15 * 60000) after.push(t);
  else rest.push(t);
  if (t.pl < 0) lastLoss = t.time;
}

Note that a loss inside the window restarts the clock. A bad streak counts as one episode.

4. Compare averages, not totals

Total P&L after a loss depends on how many trades you took. Compare the average per trade in each group.

How to read the result

  • If the after-loss average is clearly worse than the baseline over 20 or more trades, the habit costs you money. Try a rule: after a loss, no new order for 15 minutes.
  • If the two averages are close, the habit is not your problem. Look at time of day or symbol next.
  • Under about 10 trades in the after-loss group, the number is noise. Do not change anything yet.

This does not tell you what to buy or sell. It describes what already happened.

Skip the code

I put the same checks in a page that runs in your browser. You drop in the CSV, the file stays on your computer, and there is no signup: https://ab-autopsy.agentbets.workers.dev/?utm_source=devto#try

It reports closed trades, net P&L, win rate, fees, the after-loss group, your worst hour and worst symbol. It only reads the Trades section of an IBKR Activity Statement CSV. I have only tested it on a made-up file like the one above; if it fails on yours, tell me in the comments which column looked different.

Who should skip it: if you trade under about 20 times a month, there is too little data for any of these splits.
